clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant channelopathies causing recurrent, discrete episodes of ataxia rather than steady progression
EA1 is caused by KCNA1 potassium-channel mutations and features brief attacks (seconds to minutes) often with interictal myokymia, frequently triggered by startle or exertion
EA2 is caused by CACNA1A calcium-channel mutations and features longer attacks (minutes to hours) often with vertigo, nausea and nystagmus, frequently triggered by stress, exercise or caffeine
Interictal downbeat or gaze-evoked nystagmus is common in EA2 and may persist between attacks
EA2 is allelic with SCA6 and familial hemiplegic migraine, and progressive cerebellar atrophy with fixed ataxia can develop over time
Acetazolamide is a recognised prophylactic option, particularly effective in EA2; carbamazepine can help the myokymia and attacks of EA1
MRI may be normal early but can show cerebellar (vermian) atrophy in longstanding EA2
Diagnosis rests on the episodic history, family history and targeted KCNA1 or CACNA1A testing
reference.pathophysiology: The episodic ataxias are inherited ion-channel disorders of the cerebellum. EA1 results from mutations in KCNA1, encoding the Kv1.1 voltage-gated potassium channel; impaired potassium conductance causes neuronal hyperexcitability that manifests as peripheral myokymia and brief cerebellar attacks. EA2 results from mutations in CACNA1A, encoding the alpha-1A subunit of the P/Q-type calcium channel densely expressed in Purkinje cells; disturbed calcium signalling produces longer attacks of ataxia and vertigo and, over years, can lead to Purkinje cell loss and progressive cerebellar atrophy. CACNA1A's allelic relationship with SCA6 and familial hemiplegic migraine reflects a shared channel dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Transient ischaemic attacks affecting the posterior circulation
Peripheral vestibular disorders (e.g. Meniere disease, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo)
Paroxysmal movement disorders and other paroxysmal neurological syndromes
Metabolic episodic ataxias (e.g. related to pyruvate dehydrogenase or urea-cycle disorders)
additionalInvestigations: Targeted KCNA1 and CACNA1A genetic testing guided by attack duration and associated features
MRI brain to assess for cerebellar atrophy and exclude structural lesions
Electromyography to detect myokymia supporting EA1
Vestibular and oculomotor testing to characterise interictal nystagmus
Metabolic screening when a metabolic episodic ataxia is suspected
A trial of acetazolamide as a supportive diagnostic and therapeutic measure in EA2
redFlags: Focal neurological deficit or first presentation in later life suggesting cerebrovascular disease
Progressive fixed ataxia developing between attacks indicating cerebellar degeneration
Attacks with reduced consciousness or hemiplegic features prompting reassessment for hemiplegic migraine or seizures
Metabolic decompensation with encephalopathy pointing to an inborn error of metabolism
reference.prognosis: Attack frequency often lessens with prophylaxis, and many patients function well between episodes; EA1 generally does not cause fixed deficits, whereas EA2 may lead to slowly progressive cerebellar signs and atrophy over time. Overall life expectancy is typically normal.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing recurrent attacks as vestibular migraine or anxiety and missing a treatable channelopathy
Not offering a trial of acetazolamide in EA2, where it can markedly reduce attacks
Overlooking interictal myokymia or nystagmus that point to the specific subtype
Assuming a normal early MRI excludes the diagnosis or future cerebellar atrophy
references: GeneReviews: Episodic Ataxia Type 1 and Type 2
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Offer acetazolamide as prophylaxis to reduce attack frequency, particularly effective in EA2
Treat EA1 with carbamazepine or another anticonvulsant to lessen attacks and interictal myokymia, and use 4-aminopyridine as an alternative prophylactic in EA2
Advise avoidance of individual triggers, such as startle and exertion in EA1 and stress, exercise, caffeine and alcohol in EA2
Provide vestibular and balance physiotherapy with falls-prevention advice for recurrent ataxia and nystagmus
Monitor EA2 for slowly progressive cerebellar atrophy and manage coexisting migraine, given the allelic link with familial hemiplegic migraine
Offer genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant KCNA1 and CACNA1A inheritance and arrange family testing, coordinated through neurology and clinical genetics
